gaps.description: Numerical durability estimates for clinical depression stop at 12 months, and even those come from subthreshold samples (g=0.27). The 6- and 12-month guided vs unguided estimates in the IPD network meta-analysis and the long-term results of the 2013 meta-analysis were not retrieved, so their numbers are unknown to us. Residual gaps are follow-up beyond 12 months, relapse timing, and how to keep a comparison once waitlist controls are treated.
gaps.proposed_rq: In adults with diagnosed major depression, how much of the post-treatment reduction in PHQ-9 from internet CBT remains at 12, 24 and 36 months, and when do relapses occur?
gaps.method: First extract the 6- and 12-month estimates from the existing IPD and meta-analyses, then run a pre-registered IPD meta-analysis of trials with at least 12-month follow-up, modelling PHQ-9 trajectories and time to relapse. Add a 24-36 month registry-linked follow-up of a completed iCBT trial cohort.
gaps.data: IPD from the iCBT depression trials in the existing IPD consortia (13-42 trials) plus original trial authors' long-term data. Cohort follow-up could use IAPT or primary-care records and outcome questionnaires.

gaps.description: Most depression effects come from waitlist, TAU or no-access controls, and the placebo or attention component is unquantified. The only sham-like comparison is a 1-week chatbot trial with truncated results, and the transdiagnostic app estimate is not specific to clinical depression. Small waitlist trials may overstate specific effects.
gaps.proposed_rq: How much of the effect of digital depression treatment over waitlist remains when it is compared with an attention-control or sham digital condition in clinically depressed adults?
gaps.method: Meta-regression of control type (waitlist, TAU, attention or sham) on depression effect sizes, restricted to clinical depression, plus a pre-registered three-arm RCT (iCBT vs attention-control app vs waitlist, 8-12 weeks). The primary outcome is PHQ-9 at post-treatment and at 6 months, with the attention-control arm offered iCBT after follow-up.
gaps.data: Existing trial registries and the meta-analytic databases for coding control type. The RCT needs about 300 adults with PHQ-9 of 10 or more, recruited from primary care or online.

gaps.description: Moderators of symptom outcome are essentially untested in the retrieved results. Baseline severity shows only a small interaction with a broad 'low-intensity' category, while the REEACT trial found no add-on benefit and the Swedish trial found benefit over TAU, leaving adjunct vs standalone use, setting and comorbid anxiety unresolved. The two IPD meta-analyses' moderator results were not visible.
gaps.proposed_rq: Do baseline severity, comorbid anxiety, clinical setting and use as adjunct vs standalone treatment moderate the effect of digital CBT on depressive symptoms?
gaps.method: Two-stage IPD meta-analysis with pre-specified treatment-by-moderator interaction terms on post-treatment PHQ-9, complemented by a pragmatic RCT in primary care randomising adjunct to usual care vs standalone iCBT vs usual care. Compare outcomes at 3 and 12 months.
gaps.data: IPD from the consortia behind the JAMA Psychiatry and BMJ IPD analyses, with harmonised baseline variables. The RCT needs about 450 primary-care patients with PHQ-9 of 10 or more across several practices.

gaps.description: The advantage of guided over unguided formats comes from broad mental-health meta-analyses, not from depression-specific head-to-head comparisons. The only minimal-support test, lay telephone tracking, was small and found nothing. Whether the guidance advantage lasts beyond 12 months or can be replaced by cheaper support is unclear.
gaps.proposed_rq: Among adults with depression, does clinician-guided iCBT produce larger and longer-lasting PHQ-9 reductions than iCBT with automated or lay support, and by how much?
gaps.method: Three-arm non-inferiority RCT comparing clinician-guided, automated-feedback/lay-supported and unguided iCBT, with PHQ-9 at post-treatment, 12 and 24 months. Secondary outcomes are module completion and cost per remission.
gaps.data: About 600 adults with major depression recruited through online screening or IAPT-type services, with pre-specified non-inferiority margin and sample-size calculations.

gaps.description: Deterioration is quantified only from baseline to post-treatment, and engagement is linked to benefit only correlationally. Lower education predicts both deterioration and dropout, but no study has followed deterioration after treatment ends or tested whether adapting to low-education users changes it. The causal role of engagement therefore remains untested.
gaps.proposed_rq: Does an engagement-adaptive version of iCBT reduce deterioration and dropout among lower-education adults compared with standard iCBT, including during 12 months of follow-up?
gaps.method: Two-arm RCT with an adaptive version (simplified content, scheduled prompts) vs standard iCBT, stratified by education. The primary outcome is reliable deterioration on PHQ-9 at post-treatment and 12 months, with engagement mediation analysis.
gaps.data: About 500 adults with depressive symptoms, oversampling those with primary or secondary education only. Recruit through primary care and community outreach.
